title: Treating diseases

oak.lesson: Differences between infectious and non-infectious disease
DNA, chromosomes, genes and the genome

big_idea: Different types of disease need different treatments: antibiotics for bacteria, antivirals for viruses, nutrients for deficiencies, and hormones made by transgenic bacteria for people whose bodies cannot make their own.
goals: I can explain which medicines treat which types of disease, and why antibiotics do not work on viruses.
I can explain how large amounts of human hormones are made quickly using genetically modified bacteria in a fermenter.

keywords.meaning: a substance that affects how the body works
a drug used to treat or prevent disease
a medicine that stops viruses replicating (copying themselves)
a disease caused by faulty genes that a person is born with
a disease in which white blood cells attack the body's own cells
a hormone made in the pancreas that lowers blood glucose
contains DNA from more than one species
a large container in which microorganisms are grown
kill all the microorganisms in or on something

misconceptions: Antibiotics cure any infection, including colds and flu. Antibiotics kill bacteria only; colds and flu are caused by viruses, which need antivirals or the body's own immune system.
'Drug' only means an illegal substance. In science a drug is any substance that affects how the body works, so every medicine is a drug.
Transgenic bacteria are 'half human'. Only one human gene (a short section of DNA) is added to the bacterium's DNA, enough to make one protein.

slides.subtitle: Which medicine for which disease, and how do bacteria make human insulin?
slides.notes: Lesson 4 of 9C. Lessons 1 and 2 covered types of disease and immunity. Today: treating disease, from antibiotics to transgenic bacteria. The fermenter links to 9Cc in the Student Book.

slides.title: Do Now: which treatment?
prompt: 1. An ear infection is caused by bacteria. Would you give an antibiotic or an antiviral?
2. Scurvy is caused by too little vitamin C. How would you treat it?
3. A vaccine prevents a disease. Can it treat someone who already has it?
slides.notes: Four minutes, in books. Antibiotic (kills bacteria); give vitamin C in the diet (fresh fruit and vegetables); no, a vaccine makes memory cells before infection, it is prevention not treatment. Keep answers on the board for the Learn slides.

slides.title: Today
slides.notes: Read each goal aloud. Point out the key words box on the worksheet. The Chinese key words version has the same words with Chinese beside them.

slides.title: The forgotten dish
slides.question: In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould had killed the bacteria growing around it on a dish he had forgotten to wash up. What had the mould made?
slides.caption: Penicillium mould stops bacteria growing on an agar plate
text: Talk to a partner: why might a mould make a substance that kills bacteria?
slides.notes: The mould (Penicillium) made penicillin, the first antibiotic. Moulds and bacteria compete for food, so a chemical that kills bacteria gives the mould an advantage. Antibiotics have saved millions of lives since the 1940s, but they only work on bacteria.

slides.title: Drugs and medicines
slides.caption: Antibiotic capsules
text: A drug is any substance that affects how the body works.
Medicines are drugs used to treat or prevent disease.
Antibiotics kill bacteria. Antivirals stop viruses replicating.
Vaccines prevent infections. Deficiency diseases are treated by adding the missing nutrient to the diet.
slides.key_idea: Antibiotics do not work on viruses.
slides.notes: Every medicine is a drug, but not every drug is a medicine (caffeine affects the body but does not treat disease). An antibiotic for flu does nothing and can help bacteria become resistant. Other drugs treat lifestyle diseases such as heart disease.

slides.title: Diseases we cannot cure
text: Genetic disorders: faulty genes from birth, e.g. sickle cell anaemia. Treatment may last a lifetime.
Autoimmune diseases: white blood cells attack the body.
Type 1 diabetes: the insulin-making tissue in the pancreas is destroyed. High blood glucose damages organs.
slides.key_idea: Some diseases cannot be cured, but a missing hormone can be replaced.
slides.notes: Remind students of the five types of disease from Lesson 1. Insulin makes cells take up glucose (Lesson 3); without it, glucose stays in the blood at high levels and damages blood vessels, eyes and kidneys. People with type 1 diabetes inject insulin several times a day. Where does that insulin come from? Next slide.

slides.title: Transgenic bacteria
slides.caption: An industrial fermenter
text: In the past, growth hormone was taken from dead bodies and insulin from cattle: slow and expensive.
Now the human gene for the hormone is cut out of a chromosome and put into the DNA of bacteria.
The transgenic bacteria make the human hormone.
Transgenic means the organism contains DNA from more than one species.
slides.key_idea: A human gene in a bacterium makes the bacterium produce a human protein.
slides.notes: Genes are sections of DNA (9A). Because every living thing uses the same DNA code, a human gene works inside a bacterium. Genetically modified means the DNA has been altered by scientists; it is transgenic only if DNA from another species was added. Removing a gene makes a GM organism that is not transgenic.

slides.title: Inside a fermenter
slides.text: Transgenic bacteria are grown in large fermenters so that they reproduce quickly and make a lot of hormone.
slides.key_idea: Aseptic: the fermenter and everything put into it are sterilised, so no other microorganisms can grow.
slides.notes: Work round the diagram: steam sterilises the fermenter before use; nutrients (including carbohydrates to feed on) and acid or alkali to keep the pH steady go in at the top; filtered air supplies oxygen for respiration; stirring paddles keep the bacteria from sinking and mix nutrients, oxygen and heat; the water jacket keeps the temperature at the best value for the enzymes; probes check temperature and pH; the hormone is harvested at intervals.

slides.title: Quick check
slides.instruction: Mini whiteboards. One answer each, then we check.
questions: Why is a medicine a drug?
Would an antibiotic cure flu? Yes or no, and why.
In which organ is insulin made?
Why is the air bubbled into a fermenter filtered first?
slides.notes: Answers: a drug is any substance that affects how the body works, and medicines do that to treat or prevent disease; no, flu is caused by a virus and antibiotics only kill bacteria; the pancreas; contains DNA from more than one species; to remove microorganisms from the air so they do not contaminate the fermenter.

slides.title: Your turn: treating disease
steps: Core: match the medicines to their meanings, then tick the right treatment for each disease.
Core: complete the fermenter gap fill with the word bank.
Stretch: why medicines are drugs; how transgenic bacteria make growth hormone; type 1 diabetes and organ damage.

Finished? Answer the My thinking question about antibiotic resistance.
slides.footer: Say the type of disease first, then the treatment: that is the logic the examiner wants.
slides.notes: Common error: giving an antibiotic for every infection. Check the treatment table first. For Stretch 2, students should mention cutting the human gene from a chromosome, putting it into the bacterial DNA, and the bacteria then making the hormone.

slides.title: No antibiotics for a cold
slides.prompt: A patient with a bad cold asks the doctor for antibiotics. The doctor says no. The patient is annoyed. What should the doctor say to explain?
frames: A cold is caused by a ___, and antibiotics only kill ___.
Taking antibiotics when they are not needed can ___.
slides.notes: Expected: colds are caused by viruses; antibiotics kill bacteria, so they would not help; using antibiotics when not needed lets bacteria that survive become resistant, so the medicine stops working for everyone; rest, fluids and letting the immune system (Lesson 2) deal with it. Antivirals exist for some viruses but not usually for colds.

slides.title: Exit ticket
questions: What is the difference between an antibiotic and an antiviral?
Give one reason why a fermenter is sterilised before use.
slides.notes: Answers: antibiotics kill bacteria, antivirals stop viruses replicating; contains DNA from more than one species; so that no other microorganisms grow in it, which could be harmful or reduce hormone production.

slides.title: What we learned
slides.next: Medians and quartiles: how scientists use statistics to work out who a medicine helps in a clinical trial.
points: Medicines are drugs used to treat or prevent disease: antibiotics kill bacteria, antivirals stop viruses replicating.
Genetic disorders and autoimmune diseases cannot be cured, but missing hormones such as insulin can be replaced.
Transgenic bacteria carry a human gene and make the human hormone.
Fermenters give bacteria the best conditions: sterile, with nutrients, filtered air, stirring and a steady temperature and pH.

core: medicines: drugs used to treat or prevent disease; antibiotics: drugs that kill bacteria; antivirals: drugs that prevent viruses replicating; vaccines: substances that make us immune to particular diseases; insulin: a hormone that makes cells take up glucose from the blood.
ear infection: antibiotic; flu: antiviral; scurvy: add a nutrient (vitamin C); type 1 diabetes: inject a hormone (insulin); measles before infection: vaccine.
fermenter; sterilised; microorganisms; Filtered; Stirring; jacket.
stretch: A drug is a substance that affects how the body works; medicines affect how the body works in order to treat or prevent disease, so they are drugs.

Secure answer: the human gene for growth hormone is cut out of a human chromosome (a gene is a section of DNA). It is put into the DNA of bacteria, so the bacteria now contain DNA from two species (they are transgenic). The bacteria are grown in a fermenter and use the human gene to make human growth hormone, which is then extracted.

Secure answer: insulin makes muscle and liver cells take up glucose from the blood. Without insulin, glucose stays in the blood and the level becomes very high, which damages organs such as the kidneys, eyes and blood vessels. It is treated by injecting insulin (made by transgenic bacteria).
challenge: a) To supply oxygen so the bacteria can respire (aerobically) and release energy for growth. b) Any two of: nutrients including carbohydrates are added for the bacteria to feed on; a water jacket keeps the temperature at the best value for the enzymes; acid or alkali is added to keep the pH constant; stirrers keep the bacteria from sinking and mix the nutrients and oxygen evenly; oxygen is supplied. c) The fermenter and everything that goes into it are sterilised (steam kills all microorganisms), and the air is filtered. This stops other microorganisms growing, which could be harmful (contaminate the hormone) or compete with the bacteria and reduce hormone production.

Secure answer: a genetically modified organism is one whose DNA has been altered by scientists. If a gene is removed (cut out of the DNA) rather than added, the DNA has been changed but no DNA from another species has been put in, so the organism is genetically modified but not transgenic.
exit: Antibiotics kill bacteria; antivirals stop viruses replicating (they do not work on bacteria, and antibiotics do not work on viruses).
The organism contains DNA from more than one species.
So that no other microorganisms grow in it, which might be harmful or reduce the amount of hormone made.
answers.my_thinking: Open answer. Good answers use natural selection (9A): among the bacteria, a few have variations that let them survive the antibiotic; if antibiotics are used often, these survive and reproduce, so resistant bacteria become common and the medicine stops working. Using antibiotics only when needed slows this down.
